Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dil . ov. h OPINION MAR 10 2025 MS. CELINE DIALA FABELLA celinefabeIIa13@gmaiI.com Dear Ms. Fabella: This refers to your request for an opinion on a matter concerning the operation of peryahan near a place of worship, hospital or school. Below is the issue submitted for our opinion, quoted hereunder in toto: Nagtatanong po ako/kami kung ano pong batas patungkol po sa pagpapatayo ng mga peryahan sa tabi ng mgasimbahan, ospital, o mga eskwelahan. Pinapayagan po ba ito ng saligang batas o inirerespeto ng mga may katungkulansa bansang Pilipinas? Ang lugar po na ito na pinagtayuan ng peryahan ay sa Brgy Guindapunan Palo Leyte, katabi mismo ng kapilya ng Iglesia ni Cristo na katapat din ng kapilya ng Mormons.Nakakalungkot po isipin na sa maraming lugar sa Pilipinas ay may ordinansa sila na ang pagtatayuan ng peryahan ay may kaukulang sukat ng layo sa mga simbahan ng kahit anong relihiyon na dito po sa amin ay hindi naipatutupad.TuIad po sa amin na may gabi gabi po kaming pagpapanata at panalangin sa kapilya para sa pinaghahandaang paggunita sa ANIBERSARYO po ng Iglesia ni Cristo sa July 27. Gayun din po ay may mga oras at araw po kami ng mgapagsamba tuwing huwebes umaga at gabi at linggo ng umaga. Gayun din po para sa pagrespeto po sa mga Kapatid nating Mormons members. Carnival fairs or amusement parks, which are traditionally referred to as "peryahan" or "perya" usually include a collection of rides and offers a variety of games of chance that entertain and caters to adults, teenagers and children. Since these places continue to serve as places of recreation and leisure, "peryahans"have continued to be visited by many Filipinos. Notably, there is no national law regulating such establishments but these activities are considered legal and solely subject to the regulatory powers of local government units (LGUs) concerned. LGUs have the authority to issue permits to operate to amusement parks pursuant to Sections 444 (b)(3)(iv) and 455 (b)(3)(iv) of R.A. No. 7160 or the Local Government Code (LGC) of 1991, on the power of the city/municipal mayors to issue business permits for businesses or any activity put up within their jurisdiction. Additionally, each LGU—whether a barangay, city or municipality—typically has its own ordinance regulating the operation of amusement parks, rides, and attractions. This is in accordance with the General Welfare Clause under the LGC which mandates LGUs "Matino, Mahusay at Maaasahan" Trunkline NO. (02) 8876 3454

to maintain peace and order, and preserve the comfort and convenience of their inhabitants. Considering the foregoing discussions, whether the law allows the establishment of "peryahan", would largely depend on the terms and conditions of the mayor's or business permit issued and on the provisions of the ordinance enacted by the concerned LGU. Nonetheless, if the presence of "peryahan" is already causing unnecessary disturbance, the law provides for legal remedies to protect the public and maintain peace and order in the community. First, the Civil Code of the Philippines also provides a remedy under its provisions on nuisance. According to Article 694, "a nuisance is defined as any act, omission, establishment, business, condition of property, or anything else which: (1) Injures or endangers the health or safety of others; or (2) Annoys or offends the senses; or (3) Shocks, defies or disregards decency or morality; or (4) Obstructs or interferes with the free passage of any public highway or street, or any body of water; or (5) Hinders or impairs the use of property." Based on case law, however, the term "nuisance" is deemed to be "so comprehensive that it has been applied to almost all ways which have interfered with the rights of the citizens, either in person, property, the enjoyment of his property, or his comfort." 1 One of the remedies for nuisance includes its abatement which can be done: (l) extrajudicially, meaning the person suffering from the nuisance can take matters into their own hands, provided they do so without causing damage; and (2) judicially, meaning you can file a civil action in court to have the nuisance removed Secondly, you may also check whether your LGU has an ordinance that regulates peryahan. Violators of local ordinances can be fined or subjected to penalties, and local officials are authorized to enforce these rules. This opinion is based solely on the facts and representations you have narrated in your letter and our appreciation of the same. Further, this opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have addressed your concern accordingly. Thank you. Very truly yours, BY AUTHORITY OF THE SECRETARY: ATTY. ROMEO P. B NITEZ Undersecretary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs OUSELLNRPB/LLLS-LRALLD/jvpr AC ENTERPRISES v.
